list.listitem: Initial evaluation should include a careful history and physical examination and an ECG.C
CNS imaging, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring are not indicated for all patients and should be guided by specific findings of the history and physical examination.C

Patients with syncope who are older than 45 years, or with a history of congestive heart failure, ventricular arrhythmia, and/or an abnormal ECG (excluding sinus bradycardia, tachycardia, or nonspecific ST-T changes) have a greater 1-year mortality.B

Serious outcomes following syncope are unlikely if the following risk factors are absent: systolic blood pressure less than 90, shortness of breath, ECG with new changes or nonsinus rhythm, a history of congestive heart failure, or hematocrit less than 30%.B
Treatment is individualized and may include education, midodrine, fludricortisone, or in carefully selected patients a pacemaker.B

background.definition: Syncope is a common complex symptom defined by a transient loss of consciousness, usually accompanied by falling, and with spontaneous recovery. Carefully differentiate syncope from other conditions that may cause a loss of consciousness or falling such as vertigo, coma, dizziness, and seizures.

list.listitem: Syncope occurs in 6.2 per 1000 persons per year.

Incidence increases with age: 11 per 1000 persons per year at age older than 70 years; 17 per 1000 persons per year for men older than 80 years; and 19 per 1000 persons per year for women older than 80 years.
There is a 42% chance of a syncopal event during the life of a person living 70 years.
In the United States, $2 billion a year is spent on hospitalization of patients with syncope.
Reflex mediated: common faint or vasovagal, situational (cough, micturition, swallow, and defecation), visceral pain, postexercise, postprandial, and neuralgia.
Systemic mastocytosis (associated with flushing, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and urticaria pigmentosa).

Orthostatic hypotension: primary autonomic failure, multiple system atrophy, Parkinson's disease with autonomic failure, secondary autonomic failure syndromes such as diabetic or amyloid neuropathy, medication and alcohol induced, volume depletion such as hemorrhage, diarrhea, and Addison's disease.
Overly aggressive BP targets, especially for frail patients.

Cardiac structural: valvular disease (aortic stenosis), acute myocardial infarction/ischemia or coronary spasm, obstructive cardiomyopathy, acute aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism/pulmonary hypertension, tamponade, pericardial disease, and atrial myxoma.

Cardiac arrhythmia: sinus node dysfunction, atrioventricular conduction system disease, paroxysmal supraventricular and ventricular tachycardias (VTs), long QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome, pacemaker or implantable defibrillator dysfunction, and drug-induced proarrhythmia.

Pulmonary embolism has been described in several studies, but is an uncommon cause. While one study in a highly selected population found a 20% prevalence among patients hospitalized for syncope, a systematic review and a large registry study both found that the incidence of PE as the cause for syncope was less than 2%.
Neurologic: migraine, transient ischemic attacks, seizures, and vascular steal syndromes.
Psychiatric.

In patients with cognitive impairment, a systematic review concluded that patients taking cholinesterase inhibitors were less likely to fall but more likely to experience syncope than adults who take placebo.
The underlying mechanism in all syncope events is a transient global cerebral hypoperfusion.

A systematic review of 5 variable quality trials with 12,042 participants found evidence to support predonation water to prevent vasovagal syncope in blood donors (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.70-0.89). Active muscle tension was not effective.B
An RCT with 906 subjects concluded that drinking water before vaccination does not prevent postvaccination presyncope in adolescents.

An RCT of 332 adolescents found that they are less likely to experience presyncope when receiving intramuscular vaccinations when using a vibrating cool pack device plus distraction with video games than when subjected to usual care. Whether this is better than using topical lidocaine plus procaine is unclear.
A well-performed history and physical examination can often identify the cause of syncope and should drive the diagnostic evaluation.C
A standard 12-lead ECG is helpful to risk-stratify patients with syncope.AC

Routine laboratory testing and additional investigative testing such as cranial CT or cardiac echocardiography should not be routinely performed; such testing should rather be guided by specific findings of the history or physical examination.C

Differential.Differential_Features: No cardiac disease, long history, proper circumstances
Standing, temporal relationship, autonomic dysfunction, new/changed medication dose
Structural heart disease, during exertion or supine, palpitations or no symptoms before, family history of sudden death

list.listitem: Population-based studies have demonstrated that the history and physical examination identified the cause of syncope in almost half the cases in which a diagnosis was made. The history and examination, if not diagnostic, may suggest an evaluation strategy. See for an overview of different types of syncope.

The history should include circumstances just before the event:position, activity, predisposing factors; circumstances at the onset of the event; and during and after the syncopal event. Interviewing witnesses is only helpful for the patient's medical history and for confirmation of circumstances surrounding the event.
Use this interactive calculator to determine the accuracy of signs and symptoms for cardiac syncope in patients presenting with syncope.

Brief tonic-clonic activity may accompany syncope of any etiology and is seen in up to 15% of syncopal patients. Falls caused by syncope most likely result in anterior tongue lacerations; lateral tongue biting is specific for true tonic-clonic seizures. Absence of a tongue bite is not sensitive enough to have diagnostic significance.

Know the patient's medical and family background: family history of sudden death; pre-existing cardiac disease.neurologic conditions such as parkinsonism, epilepsy, and narcolepsy; metabolic disorders including diabetes, medications (in particular antihypertensive, antianginal, diuretic, antidepressant, antiarrhythmic, or QT prolonging); and the number of syncopal spells with the time from the first episode.

Check orthostatic and bilateral blood pressures. Finding an orthostatic drop within the first minute after standing more accurately predicts dizziness and future adverse events than at 3 minutes. Perform a complete cardiovascular examination looking for signs of valvular disease, rhythm disturbance, signs of ischemia, outflow obstruction, pulmonary embolism, right ventricular dysplasia, and aortic dissection. Complete a neurologic examination looking for signs of a focal neurologic deficit.

Pulmonary embolism: this is a relatively rare cause of syncope (0.3%-2.0%). Consider it in patients with tachypnea, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain, lower extremity symptoms, or risk factors for venous thromboembolism.

Cardiac syncope: syncope during supine position, a prodrome of abdominal discomfort, convulsions, and syncope during effort are all helpful at ruling in cardiac syncope in patients with suspected heart disease. Palpitations are a good predictor of cardiac syncope in patients who otherwise do not have any suspected heart disease.
In patients with aortic stenosis, severe aortic stenosis is predicted by the presence of effort syncope, slowly rising carotid pulse, and mid-systolic peak intensity of the murmur.
A prodrome >10 seconds and a history or 3 or more syncopal episodes are only modestly helpful in diagnosing neurally mediated syncope in patients without heart disease.

Initial evaluation should include ECG for most patients. If heart disease is suspected, order echocardiogram and prolonged ECG monitoring. Order the latter for any patient with very frequent episodes of syncope and any patient with clinical or ECG features that suggest cardiac syncope (). The type of prolonged ECG monitoring ordered should be based on the frequency of syncopal events. If the diagnosis remains uncertain but the suspicion for a cardiac cause remains high, consider electrophysiologic testing.

In a series of 3416 patients 60 years or older with syncope presenting to 11 EDs, 3% were discharged and experienced a serious cardiac arrhythmia within 30 days. ECG predictors of subsequent serious cardiac arrhythmia included non-sinus rhythm, multiple PVCs, first degree AV block, complete LBBB, short PR interval, and or findings consistent with ischemia.
A prolonged period of ECG monitoring in the ED (>12 hours) is more accurate for identification of subsequent serious events than a shorter period.

When interpreting echocardiograms, findings diagnostic for syncope include severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with outflow tract obstruction, severe pulmonary hypertension, and left atrial myxoma or thrombus with protrusion and outflow tract obstruction.
If syncope is accompanied by palpitations, order echocardiography and prolonged ECG monitoring. If ischemic heart disease is suspected, add stress testing.

Especially in older patients with dyspnea or other signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolism, consider CT to evaluate for that condition. A study of 2584 patients presenting with unexplained syncope found that 3.5% had a pulmonary embolism as the cause. However, a subsequent systematic review of 12 other studies (n = 7583) found that only 0.63% of persons with unexplained syncope were diagnosed with PE. A multi-national study of 1.7 million adults presenting to ED's with syncope identified PE in 0.06% to 0.55% during first evlauation and a 0.3% to 1.4% presence of any thromboembolism (VTE) at 90 days. Rates of VTE at 90 days were higher in the hospitalized population 0.75% to 3.9%. Routine evlaution for PE is not warranted in all patients that present with syncope.
Order CBC and electrolytes only if significant volume contraction or blood loss are clinically suspected (ie, patient with blood per rectum).

High sensitivity cardiac troponin testing has limited diagnostic and predictive abilities in identifying high risk syncope patients. Very high or low BNP values can rule in or rule out cardiac syncope in about 30% of older patients with unexplained syncope. See this diagnostic calculator to interpret troponin and BNP as predictors of 30 day mortality or serious cardiac event.

In patients with recurrent or severe syncope in whom cardiac disease is not suspected, tilt-table testing and carotid massage (if age older than 40 years) are useful. Do not perform massage in persons with possible carotid artery disease (although a study of carotid sinus massage in 694 octagenerians did not result in any serious complications). Perform massage in both supine and upright positions for 5 to 10 seconds with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring. The test is considered positive if syncope is reproduced during or immediately after the massage and asystole is longer than 3 seconds or systolic blood pressure falls more than 50 mm Hg. Tilt-table testing may also be helpful for patients who have high-risk occupations (ie, airline pilot). It is contraindicated in patients with severe left ventricular outflow obstruction, in the presence of critical mitral stenosis, known critical proximal coronary artery, or known critical cerebrovascular stenosis.
A systematic review concluded that heads-up tilt table testing was safe and accurate in older adults, with good specificity (85% to 100%) and a high detection rate when used with nitroglycerin.

If autonomic failure or Parkinson's disease are suspected, refer the patient for evaluation by a neurologist. If the patient has psychiatric comorbidities and a nonorganic cause of syncope is suspected, consider psychiatric evaluation.

An implantable loop recorder and event monitor are options for patients who have persistent syncope despite a negative evaluation as described above. A systematic review found no effect on mortality, but did find a greater likelihood of making an etiologic diagnosis with addition of an ILR than with a conventional diagnostic work-up.

EEG and MRI or CT are not generally helpful in the evaluation of syncope. They are only recommended if epilepsy is likely or if there are other symptoms on neurologic examination suggestive of CNS disease. In 1 series of 292 patients, only 2 had abnormal CT findings and a normal neurologic examination. In a systematic review of 15 studies with 6944 patients, the likelihood of a neurologic study providing the diagnosis were 1.3% for EEG, 1.2% for CT, 3.7% for MRI and 2.4% for carotid ultrasound.
Carotid Doppler studies in persons with syncope are unlikely to be useful and are not routinely recommended.
A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated that predicts the likelihood of a bad outcome in patients with syncope ().
The OESIL score also provides the prognosis of patients with syncope, based on age, history of CV disease, presence of a prodrome, and abnormal ECG.

The San Francisco Syncope Rulehas been developed and validated in several populations. Although the accuracy varies somewhat in different studies, it appears most useful when the ECG is interpreted by the treating physician. Low-risk patients have less than 1% risk of serious adverse events within 30 days of syncope.
The Italian Lazio rule and ROSE scores are other options for risk stratification.
An individual patient meta-analysis, though, found that overall clinical judgement was as good as the clinical decision rules in identifying serious outcomes in the month after an episode of syncope.

The Canadian Syncope Risk Score ranges from -2 to 10 points, and classifies the 30 day risk of arrhythmia ranging from 0.2% to 75%. It was validated in a study of 3819 patients in 9 emergency departments in Canada.
The EGSYS risk score predicts the likelihood that a patient with syncope has cardiac syncope.
See for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient with syncope and for an overview of the clinical presentation of different types of syncope.

Consider hospitalization for patients with suspected or known significant heart disease, ECG abnormalities or arrhythmia, cardiac ischemia or evidence of structural cardiac disease, exercise-induced syncope, syncope causing severe injury, family history of sudden death, stroke or focal neurologic changes on examination, severe orthostatic hypotension, if new or unexplained breathlessness, and if pacemaker implantation is planned. In patients hospitalized for a first syncopal event without a low Wells score and normal d-dimer, consider CT angiography or ventilation-perfusion scan. An observation unit with a standardized protocol may lead to substantial cost savings.

Individuals with syncope from a cardiac, neurologic, or idiopathic cause are at increased risk of death. Vasovagal syncope has a benign prognosis. The risk of death in patients with a cardiac cause of syncope is the same in patients with or without known cardiovascular disease.
If possible, stop drugs that may lower blood pressure or slow the heart rate.B
Midodrine has moderate evidence of benefit for patients with frequent or recurrent syncope.B
Consider a pacemaker for carefully selected patients with frequent recurrent syncope, especially if asystole documented by event loop recorder or tilt testing.B
In patients with reflex vasodepressor therapy, stopping drugs that may lower blood pressure, if possible, reduces the likelihood of recurrent syncope.

A systematic review identified 11 studies with 593 patients studying midodrine in patients with orthostatic hypotension and recurrent syncope. The 5 studies examining recurrent syncope found a reduction in recurrence (NNT = 3). Pilomotor reactions are common, occurring in about 1 in 3 patients.

A randomized trial identified 210 patients with a median of syncopal episodes in the past 9 years. They were randomized to fludrocortisone or placebo, with a trend toward fewer recurrent episodes in the active treatment group (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.46-1.03). A post hoc analysis limiting to the period at least 2 weeks after the medication was started found a greater benefit (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28-0.89).

A study identified patients with til-table positive syncope, no major psychiatric comorbidity, but high anxiety levels. In this group (n = 60) those randomized to fluoxetine were more likely to be syncope free and have fewer presyncopal events.
Midodrine has moderate evidence of benefit. Start at 5 mg three times daily during waking hours and increase to 10 mg TID if needed.
Atomoxetine and compression stockings are being studied for recurrent vasovagal syncope.

A study randomized adults with 2 or more episodes of vasovagal syncope in the past year to thigh high elastic compression stockings or sham stockings. The active intervention had no effect on recurrence of vasovagal syncope.
Patients should be instructed in the importance of adequate hydration, including bolus water drinking, and instruction on how to sit up and stand slowly to avoid syncope.
For patients with frequent, recurrent vasovagal syncope a pacemaker can be considered.

The SPAIN study was an RCT (n = 43) found that dual-chamber pacing with closed loop stimulation significantly decreased the number of episodes of syncope and the time to first episode in adults with at least 5 episodes of cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope, including 2 in the previous year.

A study randomized 167 patients 40 years and older with at least two unpredictable severe reflex syncope events in the past year and tilt-induced syncope with an asystolic pause >3 seconds to active or inactive dual-chamber pacemaker. The active pacing group was significantly likely to experience a recurrence in the following 11 months (16% vs 53%, p <0.001, NNT = 3).

ACC/AHA guidelines found limited evidence for pacing as a treatment for syncope, and recommend that it only be considered in patients with recurrent syncope and asystole confirmed by event loop recorder.

Predictors of a serious short-term event, defined as death, arrhythmia, major bleed, or stroke, were elevated BUN, history of heart failure, hypotension on admission to the ED, a history of arrhythmia, older age, and elevated troponin.B
The Canadian Syncope Arrhythmia Risk Score ranges from -2 to 8 points, and classifies the 30 day risk of arrhythmia ranging from 0.2% to 75%.B

cell.label: Diagnostic such as polypharmacy in older patients, vasovagal syncope, situational syncope, and orthostatic hypotension.
Suggestive such as aortic stenosis, pulmonary embolism, neurologic symptoms, or family history of syncope or sudden death.
Obtain specific testing such as echocardiography, d-dimer, lung scan, CT, cardiac catheterization, or EEG.
Known or suspected heart disease (abnormal ECG, exertional symptoms, or sudden syncope).
Echocardiography, exercise treadmill, monitor, or inpatient telemetry.
Loop monitor, head-up tilt-table test, psychiatric evaluation.
Age >60 years or abnormal carotid massage.*

footnotes.footnote: *Coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, valvular heart disease, cardiomyopathy, and congenital heart disease.

**May be performed in an office setting only in the absence of bruits, ventricular tachycardia, recent stroke, or recent myocardial infarction. Diagnosis carotid hypersensitivity only if clinical history is suggestive and masage is diagnostically positive.

Data from Miller TH, Kruse JE. Evaluation of syncope. Am Fam Physician. 2005; 72: 1492-500; and Linzer M, Yang EH, Estes NA 3rd, Wang P, Vorperian VR, Kapoor WN. Diagnosing syncope. feature.caption: A Clinical Decision Rule to Predict the Likelihood of Cardiac Arrhythmia or Death.
Characteristics of Different Types of Syncope.

tr.td: Usually no history of cardiac disease
Typically occurs after triggering event or prolonged standing, especially in hot crowded place, or after exertion
May be related to meals or occurs after meals
Patients often have a long history of syncope or presyncope
May occur with carotid sinus pressure (eg, tight collars) or after defecation, cough, urination, or swallowing
Occurs after changing position, ie, sitting or lying to standing
May also occur after standing in hot, crowded place
May be associated with autonomic neuropathy or Parkinson's disease
Usually accompanied by abnormal ECG or evidence of structural heart disease
Typically occurs during exertion and may be preceded by palpitations or chest pain
May be family history of sudden death
Consider when syncope occurs with arm exercise
Consider if difference in blood pressure between arms
